utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If I could remind you, sir, of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Topolski, I believe, still.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's good to see Your Honour again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The mists and fog wasn't more than to delay me a day but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We've been drawing up a list over here of what else comes from Jersey apart from His Honour Judge Parker. We'll provide it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand the evidence you've been given us to regarding this place, this camp, this facility, whatever one wants to call it, it seems to be clear, Witness, do you agree, that you must have made a number of visits there without Qerqiz being with you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on to deal with somebody else you spoke about last week, again on the 21st of March, again day 54 of the trial, beginning at page 25 of the transcript for Mr. Whiting, and this is Hasan Hoxha. I just want to ask you one or two questions about him, please. He was a friend; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had business dealings with him in the mid-1990s, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I caution you to be careful and to think about it, Witness, to do yourself justice, please. I repeat the question. Did you have business dealings with Hasan Hoxha in the mid-1990s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no. He was dealing in cars, and once I wanted to buy one car from him. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page -- paragraph 187, please, of your witness statement that is in front of you. Would you please turn that up. 1-8-7 you're looking for. Please tell me when you've got it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I knew Hasan Hoxha since 1973. He was also called Hasan Dobreva because he was from the village of Dobreva. He was a person that a lot of people knew. He was a tradesman and had a business with trading firms in Kosovo but he also used to work in restaurants and was a bouncer. I've seen him numerous times and we knew each other well, and during the years 1994-1997 we had some mutual business, mainly in car trading." You're just telling us, are you, that you just sold or bought one car with him? You can't even tell the truth about that, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling the truth. I'm telling you that we -- with this word mutual business, I meant we dealt in the same things, that is in cars. That is all I meant. He worked for himself. I worked for my own account. I don't know what the meaning of that word is in English. That's my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this passage or these passages in this part of your witness statement, you go on to deal with the discovery of a number of bodies by a roadside, potentially that must involve or include his. And if you look, for example, at paragraph 195, you will see there mention of driving along and seeing some bodies by a roadside. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wonder why there is no reference, that I can find anyway, to such a moment, such a horrific moment in this private and confidential and secret diary of important events that you used to keep during the war. Could you explain to us why there is no mention of this horrific event in this important document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing is horrific enough in a war. This you must understand. Everything is normal. And second, in the diary there are only notes about some days. It's not complete. And I can't tell you now why I didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest that here with this gentleman, whatever happened to him, was yet another example of you being a self-seeking opportunist, taking an opportunity to make a yet profit even out of death, I suggest. Would you be good enough, please, to look with me at paragraph 196 of your statement, the last paragraph dealing with this gentleman, 1-9-6. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is having dealt with what you assume to be his death and probably murder, having dealt with the discovery of bodies 3, 7, 11, or whatever the number was by a roadside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just looking at that paragraph, I think -- I don't know how counsel is going to proceed, but it perhaps should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting, I was just about to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Avni Sinani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So sorry. Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A friend like others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he someone you think would speak the truth about you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would he have any reason to tell lies about you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you've been testifying for an awfully long time. This is your seventh day, so I'm going to be brief but I'd ask you to please focus on my questions. You were asked a lot of questions about your prior interviews, and I'd like to go back to those prior interviews and put to you some passages that have not yet been put to you, and for this purpose I've distributed the English version of the 27th of May, 2003, transcript to the Court and to the parties. In addition, I've distributed some extracts from the 17th of June, 2003 interview. The whole interview is quite bulky but there are certain pages that I'd go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'd ask -- I don't know if the witness has before him the Albanian version of the 27th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's it. It says July 4th on the top but it's actually 27th of May. If we could go first to the 27th of May transcript and specifically to page 22 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on the Albanian, Witness, I'd ask you to turn to page 19 and go to the top of the page. And on the English it's about halfway down the page. And at the very top of the page in the Albanian, Witness, I draw your attention to this question, and the question is from the investigator: "Who was the head man in charge of all -- of all of the soldiers in Lapusnik," and the answer that you give is Qerqiz. Did you give that answer in the interview the 27th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then a little bit further down you explain further, and you say: "Well, let's say we were -- let's say we were person in charge not commanders. When Qerqiz arrived here, Ymer used to be the main person, the person in charge. Later on Qerqiz arrived, and we thought in the beginning -- we thought he came as a back-up. But after the 29th of May, Fatmir Limaj and Fehmi Lladrovci arrived. They told us that Qerqiz is the person in charge here," and then you say: "We were thinking to rebel against that." Now, did you give this answer in your interview of the 27th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you're asked some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise to interject. Your Honour, it's not proper cross-examination in my submission simply to put to a witness extracts of previous statements and ask him, Is that what you said. Your Honour, that may be onus for consistency if that's being alleged, but it's not proper cross-examination -- yes, re-examination, and I would object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a bit early yet to know exactly where this is going, but what you're putting is sound --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're going to lead after having identified a few passages to some questions that arise out of the cross-examination. Is that too generous a view of what's about to happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm putting these passages to the witness for a number of reasons. First of all, the witness -- a lot of parts of the transcript have been put to the witness and so it's a matter of completeness, just to complete the record. Secondly, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's a more important reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need some relevance arising out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the -- the counsel for both -- this specific passage addresses the evidence against Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu. Counsel for both of these two accused have suggested that the witness has completely made up this story about Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu and their roles in Lapusnik, that the witness wasn't even in Lapusnik during the months that he says he was in Lapusnik, and that they are all lies. And more specifically, Your Honour, the counsel have put to the witness that he -- and it was just put by -- by Mr. Topolski in the plainest form but it's been put repeatedly to the witness that he is lying here because he got a benefit for his case in Kosovo. And so I am putting to the witness the prior transcript, the interview which occurred before there was even a case in Kosovo to rebut the allegation that he has fabricated his story in order to get a benefit for his -- for his case in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So as I understand it, the primary point you're making is that this was his testimony before he got into difficulty with drugs and the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I would actually, I'm going to put these passages to the witness and draw the Court's attention to it, but I'm also going to move into evidence for that reason his prior interviews in May and June of 2003 for the sole purpose to rebut the allegation which is made -- been made five or six times in cross-examination that he is lying because he got a benefit for his case in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let's take this one stage at a time. We're not up to moving into evidence yet. That holds all sorts of other issues. We're just looking at whether this is a proper basis for re-examination. From what you have indicated, you may continue that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We will not at the moment look at the question of whether or not this will come into evidence. Now, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's most gracious. For the sake of clarity, it's not my recollection that on behalf of Mr. Limaj that we alleged the witness's account was that of recent invention. Of course the cross-examination was on the basis that Your Honours couldn't believe a word he said. But that's not recent invention. And what my learned friend is seeking to do is put evidence of consistency of that lie that we say exists. Your Honour, in my submission, that is wholly inappropriate for re-examination. It can't be used to bolster the credibility of a witness when in fact recent invention was not alleged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Recent invention is a convenient basis, a label upon which re-examination may be proper, but this is being advanced, as I understand, Mr. Whiting, on a different basis. That is the specific allegation which is most clearly being put in the course of cross-examination by more than one counsel to my recollection, and that is that the evidence being given here is directly influenced dishonestly by the desire to escape the consequences of having been arrested in 2003 for drug offences. And upon that basis, re-examination to demonstrate that an account consistent with material aspects of this evidence was given before arrest for drugs appears to be an appropriate basis for re-examination. Now, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I know I appear to be champing at the bit. May I just simply add for the sake of important completeness, if I may, that my suggestions were not limited to the benefit to be derived, if there be one, from escaping a sentence for drugs and guns and their combined possession. I also put, if I'm not mistaken, war crimes as well. My concern over this line, I don't go behind Your Honour's ruling of course, but it's only right that I should record what my concern is, that to seek to use this instrument to demonstrate prior consistency is unusual is the only way that I would respectfully describe it at the moment, and I know Your Honours will keep careful watch upon where Mr. Whiting is going with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm only reserving comment at this point because we haven't been mentioned. As soon as we are, I'm sure I'll be to my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I always fear that I might leave you out. No, the ruling has been given. If you would proceed, Mr. Whiting, but you're pursuing it for the basis that has been presently identified. So you will keep what is dealt with within those confines, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I think I will do that. And I won't address it now, but I -- but there are specific references that I could provide in response to what counsel has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you -- if you have that page still in front of you, you're then asked some questions about Fatmir Limaj's position, and you're asked: "What was his position?" And the answer you give, and if you could find it in the Albanian, the answer you give is: "After he assigned Qerqiz as the person in charge in Lapusnik, he also made it known he was our commander and every -- he said to us every" -- this is at the top of page 23 of the English: "Everything you might have, any information, anything to report, you have to report it to me through Qerqiz. Okay?" And then the question is: "So Fatmir Limaj is above Qerqiz?" And the answer is: "Yes." And the question: "Where was he stationed?" And the answer is: "In Klecka." Did you give those answers in your interview of the 27th of May, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it stands in that text, and this is what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could have before him the interview of the 17th of June, 2003, and would I draw the Court's attention to page 84, which has been provided. There's a little excerpt, 84 to 87, that has been provided to the Court and to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have page 84 in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, on this page in this interview, there's reference to some names - Fatmir Limaj, Qerqiz, Ismet Jashari - and then you are asked: "Can you explain to me what the position of these men were at the time?" And you say, and I won't read the answers word for word, but you say: "Ymer was responsible or in charge of us all at Lapusnik for several weeks, or for ten days, and after ten days Qerqiz came to us with two soldiers and a light machine-gun." And then on the next page, on page 85, you say: "Fatmir Limaj came towards the evening with about two others, and he gathered us all together and he said he was the commander in charge of all of us, in charge of the entire zone on the orders of the central staff. And he left his friend Qerqiz as commander in Lapusnik." Do you see those answers? Did you give those answers, sir, on the 17th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say: "We opposed this because Ymer was in charge." But then -- if you turn then to page 87, you say: "And then with the mediation of Fehmi Lladrovci, we agreed to this. We accepted Qerqiz as our commander and Fatmir as the commander of the zone." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you say that in the interview of 17th June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if I could turn, please, to page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if that could be provided to the witness. And it's been provided to the Court and to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And here you're asked on page 119, and this is from the 17th of June, 2003, interview: "How often would you say that Fatmir Limaj visited Lapusnik?" And here you say: "Maybe about ten times, ten to 15 times." And you say: "But he also came at night." And you say -- then you clarify: "I personally saw him about seven or eight times until July." Did you give those answers in your interview of the 17th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, finally I would ask you to look at page 37 to 39 of the interview of the 17th of -- no, I'm sorry. Page 23 first of the 17th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. June, 2003. This has also been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And here at the top of the page you're asked: "When you went to the -- went to the cowshed, how many prisoners were in the cowshed at that time?" And you say: "In that case there were about nine or ten." And: "Can you describe the condition in the cowshed at this time?" And your answer is: "The conditions were catastrophic." And you were asked to describe, and you said: "They were all tied up. They were tied by their wrists like animals with chains. They were all beaten, and they were all scared." Witness, did you say those things on the 17th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, finally, if -- if we could look at pages 37 to 39 of that same interview, the 17th of June, 2003. And here you're giving some more description of the prison and the cowshed. And you say at the top of the page of 37: "They didn't speak at all. They were beaten." And you're asked if they were Albanians, and you say: "Yes, they were Albanians, but they were beaten." And you say: "There was a stifling smell. They had no doubt urinated in the place. That's what the conditions were like. It was impossible to stay inside for a minute." And you're asked: "How was the floor like in the cowshed? Was there hay or --" and on the next page you say: "No. There wasn't any, but it was mud. It was nothing. It was stone." And you're asked to describe the smell, and you say: "It was like the smell of human beings, chickens and animals, and also like a lavatory. They performed their needs in their clothes." And you're asked if there's any possibility for these prisoners to move around, and your answer is: "No, not to go to the lavatory or anything." And then on the next page you say they were all tied to the wall. Sir, did you give those answers on the 17th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it's written there, this is the way I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, during your cross-examination, you described -- this is at -- this is on day 56 at page 39, line 16. You described an incident when a soldier was disarmed in Fustica who had a problem with Shukri Buja. And you said that Celiku went together with Shukri Buja and disarmed this person. And you said: "If you want me to give his name, I can do that." Counsel did not ask you for the name, but I will. Can you give us the name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to take care obviously not to mention where you've been relocated to, but you have been -- it's been repeatedly put to you by Defence counsel that you have benefited by being relocated out of Kosovo, and at one point in your cross-examination you said, "No, I'm a loser." Could you explain for the Court -- or could you answer this to me -- answer this question, please: Has it been a benefit to be relocated out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Since the 1990s, I have had opportunities to take my family and to seek asylum everywhere in Europe, but I never wanted to leave the country. In Kosovo I have my ancestry, my home, which I don't have now, and I live in very bad conditions. If you want me, I can prove it with facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that's enough. I think that's enough. Witness, you were asked some -- a number of questions on cross-examination about Rushdi Karpuzi and Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do Rushdi Karpuzi and Haradin Bala resemble each other? Do they look alike?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Rushdi Karpuzi has a longer face. They don't resemble each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in cross-examination Defence counsel put to you a part of your interview - excuse me - on the 18th of June; it's at page 245. When you said in that interview on the 18th of June, 2003 -- it's not before you. It's -- but what -- you said that they could be -- that they could be mistaken for each other, Rushdi Karpuzi and Haradin Bala, except that Rushdi Karpuzi did not have a moustache. But if they don't resemble each other, can you tell us why -- why did you say that in that interview? Why did you say that they might resemble each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which interview, please? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is -- this is back in June of 2003. You said that -- you said that they could be confused for each other. Why did you say at that time that they -- that Rushdi Karpuzi and Haradin Bala could be confused for each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said this because I thought that Haradin Bala will be allowed to be tried in freedom, that's why. But they don't resemble. Only -- this was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you were trying to help Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I thought that Haradin Bala was sick, and that was what I thought. It would be better for him to be tried at home while he was free, for as long as that could be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your answer. Is it -- is it -- are you saying -- is it your testimony that you were trying to help Haradin Bala when you said that Rushdi Karpuzi and Haradin Bala look alike?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did -- at -- in Lapusnik, did Rushdi Karpuzi have an injured foot or leg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did it affect in any way the way he walked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even now it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did it affect the way he walked during June and July of 1998 in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I said the same, I meant then and now it did affect him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'd lost track. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. I'm told because of attempts that will take some time to correct the transcription system, it will be necessary because of the redaction to have a half-hour delay for the time being. So we will resume at just after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, on cross-examination you were asked some questions about when you learned about Haradin Bala's heart condition. Can you recall if you learned about his heart condition during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I learnt about it after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Moving to another topic, and this is -- you were asked some questions about going to Rahovec, and your best estimate was that you went approximately on the 19th of July of 1998. Can you tell us how long you spent in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One night. The following morning we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you returned to where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- after that did you go back to Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified on cross-examination that you saw Isak Musliu two or three times after Rahovec. Was that -- did you see him those two or three times in Rahovec or in Lapusnik or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, that concludes your re-examination, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being so, sir, you'll be pleased to know that concludes the evidence which you will be asked to give during this hearing, so you are now at last free to leave and to return to your home and family. If you would now go with the court officer. The administrative arrangements are made outside. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. I would move into evidence the -- the prior interviews of the witness from the 27th of May, 2003, and the 17th and 18th of June, 2003, and there are three separate bases for this application. The first is that I would submit that the Defence suggested on a number of occasions, and I'll provide citations, that the witness was fabricating his evidence for -- for the Prosecution and in this courtroom in order to obtain the benefit of not being further prosecuted for his case in Kosovo, which began on the 13th of July, 2003, so, therefore, after the date of his interview. And just to provide the citations, on day 56 at page 21, it was put to the witness that he was being given a completely new -- an opportunity -- let me see if I can get the actual page. This is -- well, to be fair, this is -- deals specifically with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relocation, but it's at -- this is Mr. Mansfield: "You were provided with a completely new tune, were you not, in other words, you and your family were relocated, weren't they?" But I think the same point can be made about relocation because there's no evidence that -- relocation has also been suggested as a benefit. There are two benefits: The drug case in Kosovo and relocation, and relocation. There's no evidence that relocation was ever talked about before the dates or during the dates of these interviews. Then on day 57 at page 45, it was put to the witness that he would -- it was suggested that he would say anything to save himself or improve his own position. On page 46 of that same day, it was put to him that -- he was asked if he agreed that you've benefited. At page 59 of the same day -- and here I'm going to get it. This question was put to him: "Was your cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor and investigators, your statements, your interviews, indeed your evidence here, all come about because you could see a way of avoiding gaol for drug dealing, for possession of firearms and a hand-grenade." That's a specific reference to his case in Kosovo that began on July 13, 1998. And then finally it was put in -- well, no. On page -- today at page 21 and 22, again put to him that he has benefited from cooperating with the Tribunal, and the question at page 22: "I suggest that you have benefited by avoiding prosecution for war crimes and avoiding significant gaol time, as Mr. Whiting described it," I don't think I ever described it that way but that's how the question was put, "for heroin supplying and firearm possession. You disagree with all of that, don't you?" And then finally it was put in its most stark, plainest, clearest form at page 24 at the very end of Mr. Topolski's examination. This was put to him: "You were facing a very substantial term of imprisonment. You saw the benefit, you took it, and you are here giving the dishonest evidence you are giving. Those, sir, are my suggestions to you." So that directly links the benefit that is being asserted he obtained from the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to his case in Kosova and his dishonest testimony here. So I would submit that the prior interviews should come into evidence for the sole and limited purpose to rebut this suggestion that he has fabricated his evidence here in this courtroom in order to obtain the benefit with respect to his case in Kosova or with respect to relocation. Now, there's a second -- there are two more reasons, I would submit, that the transcript should come into evidence. The second one is that the transcripts were repeatedly put to him. Various portions of the transcripts were repeatedly put to him by all counsel. And with respect to a prior witness, the second witness who testified in this courtroom. We'll get his number in a second, but it was the second witness. The Court found that where there had been numerous references to a -- numerous references to a prior transcript that it -- it was appropriate for it to come into evidence so that the context of various statements could be evaluated. And I would draw -- for that -- that ruling is actually at page -- at day 8, page 934, 935. So that's the second reason, that there have been so many references to it, so many questions about the prior interviews and about various passages, that the Court should have avail to be it the context of those questions of the overall interview. The third reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That of course depends on whether the issues raised in cross-examination are apparently likely to be affected by context, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's -- it's very difficult -- it's very difficult to make that evaluation, and I would -- I would submit that where -- where there are so many references to it, it's likely to be the case that the context is going to be important and -- of these various references, and that seeing the overall transcript is going to be important. It may be the case that that's -- that that is -- that it doesn't prove to be very helpful, but in that case there's nothing lost. I simply would submit that it should be available to the Court as a tool in evaluating the various passages that were being put to the witness. Finally, Your Honour, there's a third reason, and that is that it was suggested to the -- it was suggested to the witness quite forcefully, and this is at page 6 of day 57, and this is from Mr. Guy-Smith, that the witness was -- his answers were being moulded by the questioner and that he was providing information that the questioner -- my -- Mr. Nicholls tells me that the witness that I was referring to, the second witness, is Witness L-7. But just to go back to my point, my third point here, that the answers were being moulded by the questioner. And -- and there was one example that was put to the witness, but it was -- but the suggestion was that this was a general practice that had occurred during the -- during the interviews. And the question at page 6 is: "Now, when he said that to you, I'm suggesting to you, sir, that this is the first time in the number of interviews that you had with the OTP that you learned and decided to mould information according to what you believed they wanted to hear." Well, I would submit that given that suggestion, it's important for the Court to have available to it the transcripts of the interviews to -- so that it can determine whether there is any basis to this suggestion that the witness moulded his answers according to what the investigator wanted to hear. The questions and answers are transcribed. It can be, I would submit, discerned from that transcript whether there is a basis to this suggestion. So that is the third reason. I would submit that each of these reasons independently justifies admission of these transcripts into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. Your Honour, I oppose the application made by my learned friend. Your Honours, of course, may remember what in my submission was a careful and thorough cross-examination by lead counsel on behalf of Mr. Limaj. The extract quoted or cited by my learned friend, when it was put to the witness, which is our case, that the witness is a person willing to say anything to save himself, of course relates to his testimony in the dock, and Your Honours will assess in due time the credibility, if any, of this witness, whether or not he is a thorough liar, or whether or not you can give even the slightest weight to what he says. But, Your Honour, that relates to his demeanour and his testimony under oath in the dock, which did you not require any other assistance from any other source to evaluate. You've had the best evidence, which is the witness before you, as my learned friend says, for seven days. So, Your Honour, that's the context. The second point is that the extracts of the interview that were put to the witness were accepted by him. Your Honour, there was no need to exhibit these interviews as previous inconsistent statements, because when extracts of interview are put to the witness, he repeatedly accepted what was stated and then sought to clarify or somehow explain. So again, Your Honour, no need at all to have recourse to any other source other than the evidence of the witness given under oath and thoroughly tested by both parties through a very lengthy examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Your Honour, the third objection is relevance. It's simply not relevant to the determination of this matter because, Your Honour, before the break you of course allowed my learned friend to read out forces of the transcript which he deemed to be relevant. Your Honour, by allowing that those extracts were thereby read into evidence. Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Limaj, I accept my learned friend read out accurately what's in the interviews. So there's no need to go beyond what my learned friend has already read into evidence. For these three reasons, I do object as a matter of principle to these -- and as a matter of application for these lengthy interviews to bother Your Honours. I say, Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Limaj, there is no need for you to look at yet more papers when you have seven days of transcripts to go through. And for those three reasons, I would oppose the application made by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I have a number of comments to make. I similarly oppose this particular application. Initially, the issue concerning this particular witness's cooperation or the benefits that he derived therefrom is something that was tested in the crucible of examination, both direct and cross-examination. The attempt to introduce statements which I think probably between the interviews as well as written statements comprise more than 350 pages of material is not only, I think, inappropriate but will be something that will of no assistance to the Chamber in making a determination with regard to whether or not this particular witness received any benefits for his cooperation, and the use of those statements for these purposes is absolutely off point. With regard to the issue of putting matters in context, I think that if the Chamber was to review the transcript, you will note that there were probably very few references to pages used, and by that I mean we probably in total discussed less than a twentieth of all the information that existed. My examination with regard to those issues was quite specific. It dealt with issues concerning identification. It dealt with issues concerning specifically the question of who was a guard. And his answers were answers that were, once again, as Mr. Khan has indicated, answers that he accepted having made at the time, and there were also issues concerning his knowledge of my client, and finally issues concerning his understanding of his purpose for being at the interview because, in fact, there were a number of places where there were off-the-record discussions for which we have no information, and indeed suggestion that were made, limited though they may be, but suggestions by the questioner that he could deviate from answers previously given which is something else that he accepted having been told. The use of the statements themselves doesn't, once again, assist in any regard, and as a matter of fact, there are a legion of subjects other than those that have been discussed here that are included in those statements that will not only be of no assistance to the Chamber but I believe will be dealing with collateral matters and matters that, quite frankly, will confuse the very issue that exists with regard to this witness, and I think in large measure that is the credibility of this witness. Is this witness to be believed or not? And that is I think primarily going to be based upon your assessment of his evidence as given both in direct and in cross-examination, and you need nothing further. The context argument, the context discussion suggested by Mr. Whiting, once again, is absolutely off point, because the context of the questions asked were in very limited areas, I believe by all parties, and could be -- in the event the Chamber needs them could be satisfied by giving the Chamber those particular pages of the interviews and transcripts, if such is necessary. I don't believe that even that is necessary. I think in large measure what the effect will be if the Chamber makes a determination that it is going to accept this suggestion is that you will have before you a vast amount of information which is absolutely irrelevant, totally off point, clearly not germane to the issues at hand, and therefore it should not be entertained by you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I, too, object to this application. May I just deal with two of the three grounds in its support advanced by Mr. Whiting first of all. In essence and in summary, and I try not to do grievous bodily harm to all his submissions, in respect to them I simply try to summarise them in this way: That his first objection is that this is to rebut the suggestion that this evidence is benefit rather than truth driven. That is a very different suggestion than the one that normally, certainly in my jurisdiction, founds this kind of application, namely the one of recent fabrication. There was no dispute in relation to those passages that I put that the record of the interviews that I put, and there were not many, were not accurately recorded. A point that Mr. Guy-Smith has already made. But fundamentally my response to point one of Mr. Whiting's is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. although not exclusively, for the most part such an application as this being in recent fabrication is not the case here, and therefore does not have a firm enough basis for the admission of this material. The second point he makes is that it puts the cross-examination in context as an evaluation tool. I think I quote him directly. With great respect, that is the purpose of re-examination. That is what it is designed to do. That is why the facility is given to the caller of the witness to have the last word with the witness. And of course one is under some pressure of time, especially when one's had a witness in a courtroom for seven days, but time is well spent, the Court may think, when re-examination is conducted into those areas that the caller of the witness wishes to clarify by contextualising, as it were, the material that's been put in cross-examination. To use this device, and I don't mean that word pejoratively, to get in the totality of the material that Mr. Whiting was perfectly free and entitled to and indeed did put in re-examination to the witness is not, we would submit, anything approaching a firm foundation for this application. Really the third point that he makes I think the suggestion that comes from Mr. Guy-Smith to the witness that the questions were moulded by the questioner is very much the same, is it not, as saying, well, look at all of this material to give some context to the questions that were asked and put. Again, we submit the perfectly proper vehicle for that is the vehicle of re-examination. Your Honour, these exhibits that my learned friend seeks to put in amount to some 300 pages of material. That of itself is not a reason not to put them in, of course, but let's be blunt about it. The effect of this is to get in untested evidence by the back door. Of course it would be said in response to this point, no doubt, we are dealing here not with juries but with professional Judges. That of course is right, and what a Judge can do is put out of his or her mind, it is said, those matters that are not properly in the Judge's mind. That's all very well, but what that does or might do, and when one is judging, one must have a eye, I respectfully submit to this point, that that must leave, must it not, a very uneasy feeling in the mind of the lay defendant who says to him or herself, Well, hold on a moment, what about all that stuff in that interview that -- take an example, I don't say this case, take another example altogether, that is wholly prejudicial to me, that no lawyer asked about, neither prosecutor nor defender. How can I be sure that if a judge reads that said about me, untried and untested, it's not in some subconscious subliminal way going to effect even to a small extent the Judge's view of the witness and, therefore, of me? The effect of this is to get in an abundance of material, I think Mr. Guy-Smith's phrase for it, that has been untested, uncross-examined, not led by my learned friend in very much the same way the same point would apply to witness statements. Your Honours, it is a submission that for the reasons we have put forward is not sufficiently grounded, we would submit, in a firm foundation to enable it to succeed. Can we really just consider finally what the position is here and what's really being said, and may I hopefully, helpfully summarise it in this way: Day one is a crime is committed, witnessed by a witness. Day two, that witness himself commits a crime. Day three, he is interviewed about the crime on day one, and of course nothing is said about the crime he's committed on day two because no one knows about it. On day three, the fact that he has allegedly committed a crime himself comes to notice, and on day four, a deal is done, putting the phrase neutrally for the moment, whereby he is not prosecuted for the crime committed on day two and he agrees to give evidence in relation to the crime that he has witnessed. Is it really to be said that all that he or she said in interview regarding the crime he or she witnessed is relevant and admissible in the trial of the perpetrator of the first crime in order in some way to place into some historical context the overall picture where the historical context has been exhaustively examined and cross-examined in this Chamber by, and I don't include myself in this, highly experienced counsel on both sides of the fence. Your Honour, that is why we have trials, to air in public and sometimes in private these very matters. It is the privacy of what is being suggested here, the admission into evidence in effect of material that has not been ventilated publicly that should, and we hope would, be the factor that defeats this application above all others. Your Honours, that's the basis upon which we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would submit that it is -- it is standard evidentiary law that if there is an allegation, and it is true in -- certainly true in my country, and I would submit that it's also true in the United Kingdom, and I believe it's also true in Australia, that if it is alleged that a witness has fabricated his testimony in court, is lying in court for a particular reason, then it is entirely proper to go to a point in time before that reason for fabrication existed to see what the witness said to see if it is consistent with that witness's current testimony and to admit into evidence the witness's prior statement given before the point in time when the reason for fabrication -- the alleged reason for fabrication occurred, but for the narrow purpose of determining whether the witness has in fact fabricated his testimony for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first half of that proposition is one which I don't think is disputed by anybody here, at least at this stage, that is, that it is proper to go to the previous earlier statement for the purpose of seeing whether there has been a material departure, and that is what occurred in both cross-examination and re-examination. It is a different question whether the past record of interview or statement ought to come into evidence, whether there's justification for that, and that is something which you might like to concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I would submit that certainly here with the system that we have where there is no jury and there is no rule against hearsay, that it should come into evidence for that very purpose. And, yes, it is true that I put certain passages to the witness from the prior interviews, but I would submit that the -- that the entire transcript should be in evidence, and not because I'm looking to get other matters in. That's not the purpose. And I would not for a moment rely on things said in those interviews which were not addressed in the courtroom. It is simply the point about the consistency of his story and certain topics, and I put to him some of the passages. It would be impossible, it would take days to put to him all the passages which touch on his testimony. He testified in direct examination for three days, and there are many points in those prior interviews which touch on those passages. It would have taken me literally a day or two to go through every single passage, and it is only for the purpose of evaluating his consistency and evaluating whether he has fabricated his testimony for the benefit of the case in Kosova or for relocation. That is the only purpose we would seek the admission, not for any extraneous matters or matters that were not dealt with in the courtroom, topics that he did not discuss here. That is not something we would at any point seek to rely on. I don't think that that would be proper, and that's not the use that we're seeking to put it to. So I think that because there's no risk of prejudice, there's no risk of -- there's no jury here, there's no hearsay rule, I think it should come into evidence so that the Court can go through and evaluate the entire transcript and all the matters that are touched on there were also touched on here in court to make a determination, as one of the counsel said, I think it was -- I can't recall which one it was, whether it was Mr. Guy-Smith or Mr. Topolski. The question is: Is this witness to be believed or not? That's the question. And I would submit that having the transcript and being able to look at all of the points where there was consistency, having that in evidence and having it just for that narrow purpose would in fact help to answer that question, which is why we are all here. The only other point I would make, Your Honour, is that with respect to my third basis, the suggestion that the witness had moulded his answers. Well, it was suggested by Mr. Topolski that that is something I could have done on re-examination. That would be impossible to go through, I would submit. You would have to go through the entire transcript to see that in fact he was not moulding his answers to respond to what the investigator wanted him to say. They weren't being -- the answers were not being fed to him. That's something that's -- it was a very broad suggestion made by Defence counsel in his questioning that this was just the first of many examples in these interviews where his -- the witness had moulded his testimony or had been encouraged to mould his testimony to fit what the investigator wanted him to hear. And the suggestion is that he's come into the court today with a moulded story, that has been moulded by the investigator, and would I submit that the transcript of the interview rebuts that allegation and that the only way to do that is to consider the transcript in its entirety for that purpose, and it's impossible to go through and pick out one or two examples. It's in a sense proving a negative. That can only be done by looking at the entire transcript. But the primary point that I would go back to is that I think this Court should have the entire transcript in order for the very narrow purpose of rebutting the allegation that this witness has fabricated his testimony because he wanted to be relocated or because he wanted the benefit of a case. And Mr. Topolski suggested that he wanted that benefit even though the case did not exist. I would submit, with all due respect, that that is extraordinarily far-fetched, that the witness before a case even existed started laying the groundwork for a deal and a benefit, and I would submit that the transcript also would refute -- also plainly refutes that notion that the witness is trying to create a future benefit for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me. May I add something because I hope it may help. Of course my learned friend could respond if he wishes to with your leave. We, the Defence bar, I mean, and I've spoken to all my learned friends about this, would accept that on the face of the record of all of these interviews, there is of course no discussion or reference to benefits at all. And therefore, if my learned friend is seeking to establish in one respect, well, it's all a bit surprising if there is any merit in what is being suggested here there is no reference to this directly or in passing, and I underline the words in the light of Mr. Guy-Smith's cross-examination, on the face of the record, we admit, of course, there is no reference to seeking a benefit, trying to gain an advantage either in relation to past or future conduct. If that in any way assists the Tribunal in seeing a way through, as it were, the social democratic view of things, see if there's a middle course, then I raise it for that so unlimited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn for a short time to consider the submissions. --- Break taken at 11.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we expect to be able to give our ruling on your motion tomorrow rather than delay longer now. We will carry on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Nicholls will be handling the next witness. The next witness is ready. If I might be excused for some time, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Bench microphones seem to have developed a particular problem. The level of intensity produces squeal, feedback. All right. Mr. Nicholls, you have a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Should be ready, Your Honour. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I just ask in terms of breaks, will we now continue to the end without a break or is there a need for a break in between somewhere, having -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. Every time I go to speak we're getting this problem. I take it others are hearing what we are hearing. Yes. We would be sitting now for about quarter of an hour before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Quarter of an hour before the break. Okay, thank you. I may say, this witness speaks English. The direct and questions will be in English, so the headphones may not be as necessary for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kereakes, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would read allowed the affirm significance on the card in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kereakes. If you would sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry that you were kept waiting for a little while this morning. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Anargyros Kereakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to start asking you some questions now first about your background, but later on we'll be moving into the time you spent in Kosovo, and I'd like to remind you to be very careful not to mention the names of any persons you might have taken witness statements from when we're in what's called open session. I will try to bring us into private session for brief moments when we need to mention names of some people, but other than that, please be careful with the names. Also, we need to try to make a -- speak more slowly than we usually do and take a short pause between questions and answers, because in these booths everything we say is being translated for the record, and that takes some time. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell me where you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Oak Lawn, Illinois, United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to briefly go through your educational and employment background before we talk about some other topics. You graduated from high school and then went through two years of college at Loyola University; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again we're going to need just a little pause between my question and your answer. Could you tell us what you studied at Loyola?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Criminal justice and psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you complete that programme?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I then became a Chicago police officer, entering the Chicago police academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What year did you enter the police academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you complete the academy?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What were your first duties as a police officer after completing the police academy in Chicago?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I had entered the Chicago police academy for the Chicago housing police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long were you in that department?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly if you can describe what your duties were as a police officer with the Chicago housing department?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I was assigned to routine patrol, answering calls for service, responding to in-progress calls. Also, I was later assigned to a tactical unit which worked gangs and narcotics in a public housing area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was your next assignment or department after the housing department?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I then left the Chicago housing department, police department, and then I accepted a position with the Chicago police department starting off again as a patrol officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What were your duties from 1994 on as a Chicago police department officer?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I started off in routine patrol and later was placed on the Tactical Unit working in various parts in the city of Chicago enforcing gang violence, also responding to any in-progress calls, assisting our detective division in routine burglaries, armed robberies, and even homicides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in August of 2000, did you go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you go that month of that year?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I volunteered for the International Police Programme Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Kosovo with that programme?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During that time were you still with the Chicago police department?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I was on a leave of absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to those two years in a little while and talk about the time you spent in Kosovo. Could you briefly bring the Trial Chamber up to date on your career since you returned from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: After my return from Kosovo, I went back to the Chicago police department. I was an instructor at the Chicago police academy, also a supervisor now holding the rank of sergeant. I volunteered for another assignment oversees, this time Indonesia, to train a special riot control team in democratic policing principles and also on tactics. I then returned to the Chicago police department once more, and this time I accepted an assignment in October of 2003 contracted to the US State Department as a close protection detail member for the US Consulate assigned to the Road-Map to Peace . My duties included protecting principles in Gaza and The West Bank. I stayed there till February, at which time I then volunteered to go to Afghanistan as the close protection member for the US Ambassador. I stayed there until December, at which time I was then transferred back to Israel as a close protection detail member for the US Consulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I just ask now: Are you currently a member of the Chicago police department?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I am currently a sergeant but I am on a leave of absence from the Chicago police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I want to turn to August 2000, the month you arrive in Kosovo. Could you please tell me what your duties were when you arrived, what units, areas you were assigned to.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Upon my arrival, I was assigned to the Kosovo Polje/Fushe Kosove police station at which time I began in routine patrol, and later I was assigned to the intelligence investigation section of our station. In February of 2001 I accepted a position with the Central Criminal Investigation Unit, otherwise known as CCIU, as a war crimes detective. I stayed there till February, for one year, at which time then I transferred to the missing persons unit and also to the regional murder squad as a detective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you first joined CCIU as an investigator, were you a team leader of any kind or were you a member of a team?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I was a member of a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During that time as a war crimes detective, as a team member with CCIU, can you describe please the types of crimes that were within your mandate and that were investigated?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: We were mandated to investigate any crimes of criminal sexual assault, kidnappings, and murders that occurred by both sides. By "both sides" I mean Serbian and Albanian in the Kosovo conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you receive any special training for this new environment that you found yourself in?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just briefly describe that training.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Upon assignment to the central criminal investigation unit, we were the -- the class that I was in was trained by a more senior detective. Mine happened to be one from the RUC, from Northern Ireland, and he was assigned to me to teach me the way that we would be keeping the case files, how we were conducting the interviews of witnesses, victims, and also to suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At some point in time were you promoted to team leader?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: I believe it was July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that 2001?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you remember, how long did you hold that team leader position?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Until I left in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe your team briefly? How many detectives or investigators were in your team that were under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Usually we had 16 to 20 detectives assigned to my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, please, what difficulties you personally and your team may have faced in investigating war crimes in Kosovo at this time.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: It seems that we never had enough manpower for all the cases that -- that we had. For example, each -- each investigator was assigned six to eight cases. That also included myself. Even though I may have been team leader, I was -- still had my own caseload. Any time -- any time that a new case would arise or a new complaint would come in, that would be another case for one of my detectives or for myself. In addition, we also were often tasked from the police commissioner to investigate any new crimes that had occurred within Kosovo. I had many difficulties often locating witnesses. Just facing -- learning who my suspects were and the victims and witnesses refusing to speak many times through the Albanian language assistants since many of them feared they would be compromised. I often had to seek out other methods of interviewing, statements, by attempting to find other languages to be used for the fear and safety of my witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What other languages did you use. Can you just tell us how you briefly went about that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: German was another language that we used. Serbian was another language, even French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us from your experience there whether these witnesses's fears were valid about using local translator staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection. Lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, no. What is your submission to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he can -- I think the foundation is laid that he was there. I'm asking if based on his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this anything to do with this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It goes to the way in which statements were obtained sometimes using different languages rather than the language, the mother tongue of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness says there were these concerns or objections by some witnesses. Is it going to help for us to explore whether there was any substance to that that's going to help this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's relevant, Your Honour, to the -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evaluating witness statements and evidence that were generated to understand a little bit of the problems that the witness may have had using local staff in order to obtain statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have from the witness that there were these problems experienced with some witnesses and that has led him to use interpreters that use other languages than Albanian. Isn't that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we uphold your objection, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about -- can you describe the level of support you received from the local police forces, the KPS?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: There were several instances where I would go to the local level, the station level and would not receive any type of support in helping to locate witnesses. I also had a fear that many of the new KPS officers were also former members of the UCK and also, too, had received directions and orders from my suspects. So to always safeguard my witnesses and the case file, I always -- not always, I usually tried to avoid the KPS department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's been 15 minutes since we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a convenient time, I take it, Mr. Nicholls. We must have the break now to enable the tapes to be changed. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you continue, Mr. Nicholls, the Chamber is in a position now to give its decision in respect of the motion that had been moved by Mr. Whiting. We'll deal with it now very briefly. The Chamber is of the view that the previous statements or records of interview should not be admitted into evidence on this occasion. The matter is to be distinguished significantly from the case where a witness is apparently hostile so that there is a major question whether the evidence given by the witness and the previous statements are at different purposes for different motivations and the question may arise of a need for detailed comparison. This is a case where the witness gave his evidence fully and freely, was then cross examined about some particular passages, and the passages appear adequately in the transcript record. They appear adequately for the particular purpose relevant to a submission of one Defence counsel that there had been some encouragement by the questioner for the witness to take a particular line or that the effect of suggestions by the questioner had been to have the witness take up a particular theme. Those parts were carefully adverted to in questioning and so appear in the transcript. We have the position where there have been particular references in this way during examination and cross-examination to a few limited particular aspects of what is an extremely lengthy set of previous interview material. I haven't looked at the number of pages, but counsel indicate it's in excess of 300. To a substantial extent, it appears the content of that material has not been thought by counsel to be relevant and has there are has not been adverted to in the course of evidence. So context does not require the Chamber have available the original, and relevance appears to suggest that the majority of it could have no relevance to our consideration of the merits of this case. We were concerned to see whether there was something in the previous ruling which had been given and which was relied upon by counsel, and it has been possible to remind us also of the circumstances of -- in which that occurred. We were there dealing with a witness, a suggestion -- well, there were a number of suggestions, but there were three previous statements, each short, and counsel for one of the accused actually moved for the admission of one of those. Counsel for the Prosecution then suggested all three ought to be received, in particular to compare the material parts of each of the three, one with the other. There was no objection by any counsel at that time, and the Chamber was persuaded to accept the three. It is not, we believe, authority for the proposition that it was relied upon before us today. It must be said that a little later in the day another Defence counsel sought to reopen the question, but the Chamber is of the view that the horse had already bolted. It is a particular case limited to that situation and not of any general indication of the Chamber's view as to what should occur. In fact, I was interested to see that the Chamber's comments include a reference in allowing those three to be admitted, include a reference that the normal practice is for those putting a previous statement to the witness to ensure that the record discloses the parts of it that are relevant to the questioning so that the whole statement itself is not needed as an exhibit. For those very brief reasons, as I have indicated, we will not accept the motion to receive previous records of interview of the last witness into evidence in this case. Now, with that interruption, I'm sorry, Mr. Kereakes, but we had to deal with an admissibility question. Mr. Nicholls, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Kereakes, I'm now going to start asking you some questions about specifically your time as a team leader at CCIU after 2001. During that time, what physical area in Kosovo was within your jurisdiction, in other words crimes? Where would you have authority to investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Anywhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you personally investigate any crimes once you became a team leader which took place in and around Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, could you describe what that case was about.

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: This case concerned victims that were kidnapped by the UCK, illegally detained, tortured and murdered for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you start this investigation from scratch yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you recall, who was the team leader before you on that case?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: That was Detective Kare Birkeland. I believe he was from Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What you received from Kare Birkeland, did you create any photo line-ups?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: Yes, did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: According to the victims and witnesses in a case, they had named offenders at which time I thought it was important to be able to go ahead and conduct a photo line-up to make sure that we would be able to locate these suspects and make sure that the identity was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you personally - and I mean physically - construct the line-ups for this case yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you have these line-ups created?

utterances.speaker: ANARGYROS KEREAKES
utterances.text: One of our other detectives was very good with the computer, unlike my skills, so at that time I wasn't very good in how to cut and paste the photographs to the line-up, so I used his services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you remember, who was the suspect in the first photo line-up that you created? What was his name?
